# Guāndì: the stories first, then the spelling

You cannot weigh an accent without knowing what it carries. Here is what **Guāndì** has been carrying.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Peach Garden.** The Romance of the Three Kingdoms opens with the oath: in a peach garden, Guān Yǔ swore with Liú Bèi and Zhāng Fēi to die on the same day as brothers.  He kept it past reason — through capture, through Cáo Cāo's gold and titles, riding a thousand miles back to his sworn lord with the general's seal hung on his gate.  Loyalty, in China, has a face, and it is his.

**Lord of the Beautiful Beard.** Held by Cáo Cāo, he accepted three conditions only: he surrendered to the Han, not to Cáo; his brother's wives would be protected; and he would leave the moment Liú Bèi was found.  He kept all three, repaying Cáo Cāo's courtesy by beheading the enemy general Yán Liáng — honor answering honor, the episode the temples never tire of carving.

**From General to Emperor.** Killed in 220 CE by Sūn Quán's men, he began as a local protective spirit at Dāngyáng; the Sui made him a Buddhist guardian; the Song emperors titled him Duke, then King; the Ming made him Emperor Guān; the Qing added "Sage," matching Confucius himself.  No other Chinese figure rose from battlefield casualty to co-Sage of the empire — the slowest, most official deification in history.

## And Here Is What the Spelling Preserves

Against those stories, the attestation: **關帝**, as Sanguozhi and Chinese folk religion record. The name means ""Emperor Guan" — the deified general Guān Yǔ, god of war, loyalty, and righteousness".


## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Guāndì
- **ASCII form:** guandi
- **Meaning:** ""Emperor Guan" — the deified general Guān Yǔ, god of war, loyalty, and righteousness"
- **Domain of influence:** War, Loyalty, Protection
- **Pantheon:** Chinese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 關帝
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 159 of 463

## The Name Travels

He is the one deity all three teachings claim: Taoism's Guān Shèng Dì Jūn (Holy Emperor), Buddhism's Sānghārāma, Confucianism's co-Sage.  The diaspora carried him everywhere — his altar stands in Yokohama's Kanteibyō, in San Francisco's oldest Chinatown temples, and in every Hong Kong police station, where officers and triads bow to the same red face: the god both sides trust because both sides fear to lie before him.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Guāndì** stands at [/guandi/](/guandi/) — [lore](/guandi/lore/), [scholars](/guandi/scholars/), [patterns](/guandi/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. What survives here cannot be shown in ASCII: a feature of the original that the fallback alphabet flattens. That is the Tier-1 test, and this name passes it without argument.
